title: Teach Me Something New
coreMove: Give the audience one useful new frame that makes the familiar worth attention again.
sourcePressure: The source treats novelty as an attention magnet when it delivers genuinely new information or a novel frame on familiar material. Robert Ballard, James Cameron, and Hans Rosling anchor discovery, exploration, and fresh data presentation.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says surprise people with cleverness. The useful version says teach one fresh, usable thing that clarifies the message.

sourceAnchors.name: Robert Ballard
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Ballard as an anchor for curiosity, discovery, and exploration
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Robert Ballard gives novelty its cleanest form: discovery that makes the room lean forward because the world has opened a little.

sourceAnchors.name: James Cameron
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Cameron as an exploration and discovery anchor in the chapter
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: James Cameron belongs where exploration turns information into a fresh view, not where spectacle tries to replace the idea.

sourceAnchors.name: Hans Rosling
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses Rosling for making dry or familiar data feel new through presentation design and motion over time
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Hans Rosling made data move, and movement let old facts feel newly visible.

hook: audience phones go down when novelty appears
counterintuition: you always have something new to say

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.audience: a utility educator speaking to homeowners who think conservation means shorter showers
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether familiar water advice becomes a new view of hidden outdoor leakage
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks which household use wastes the most water, lets the room pick showers, then reveals the night-irrigation meter traces and teaches the leak pattern
exampleSpecs.firstImage: blue meter spikes climbing across a tablet after midnight

exampleSpecs.audience: a museum educator introducing a familiar local settlement display
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether visitors learn something fresh about trade rather than seeing old pottery again
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he holds up a shard with foreign clay residue and reframes the exhibit from old objects to a map of travel and exchange
exampleSpecs.firstImage: grainy clay dust catching under a small exhibit lamp

exampleSpecs.audience: a payroll manager teaching supervisors a new overtime approval rule
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the rule feels like administrative burden or a fresh way to prevent hidden wage mistakes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she replaces the policy summary with one anonymized pay stub that shows the mistake supervisors had never noticed, then teaches the rule
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a blacked-out pay stub with one overtime line circled

exampleSpecs.audience: a public-health nurse trying to increase blood-pressure screening at a county fair
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether residents hear another warning or a new comparison that makes silent risk visible
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he shows two fair maps, one with food vendors and one with last year's high readings by booth, so the screening tent feels newly relevant
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two county-fair maps clipped to a folding table under a canvas awning

exampleSpecs.audience: a graduate researcher explaining a warehouse robot to visiting manufacturers
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether guests see another automation demo or learn a new way to measure wasted walking
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: when a visitor asks what is new, he tapes yesterday's picker path on the floor and lets the robot's shorter route reveal the idea
exampleSpecs.firstImage: yellow tape zigzagging across a polished lab floor

exampleSpecs.audience: a dietitian teaching parents who know the usual sugar warnings
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether parents learn a new frame for breakfast satiety rather than another list of forbidden foods
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he sets two breakfast receipts beside a hunger log and reframes the lesson around when children ask for food again, not just grams of sugar
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two crumpled grocery receipts weighted under a clear plastic measuring cup

skillTargets: choose a new frame for familiar material
analyze whether a fresh fact clarifies the main idea
evaluate when novelty distracts from learning

tryThisNowSpec: For one familiar point in your next talk, write what the audience already assumes, then add one fact, comparison, or frame that would make them see it differently.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
